name: Nickel-cadmium
self_discharge: About 10% per month at 20 °C, up to 20% per month at higher temperatures (Wikipedia)
summary: Nickel-cadmium cells pair a nickel oxyhydroxide positive electrode with a cadmium negative in a potassium hydroxide electrolyte and deliver 1.2 V on a flat curve. Rugged and tolerant of high discharge rates, they have been displaced in consumer use by nickel-metal hydride and lithium-ion, largely because cadmium is toxic.
body:
## How it works

A nickel-cadmium cell uses a nickel oxyhydroxide positive electrode, a metallic cadmium negative electrode and an alkaline electrolyte, commonly potassium hydroxide. The electrolyte is not consumed in the reaction, so unlike in lead-acid cells its specific gravity does not indicate state of charge. Sealed cells roll the electrode plates and separator into a spiral, the jelly-roll design, inside a metal case with a self-sealing safety valve. That construction lets a NiCd cell deliver much higher current than an alkaline cell of the same size. The abbreviation NiCad is a trademark of SAFT, though it is commonly used for the chemistry as a whole.

## Discharge behavior

Terminal voltage during discharge is around 1.2 V and decreases little until nearly the end, a flat curve that contrasts with the sloping discharge of alkaline cells. A fully charged cell reads 1.25 to 1.35 V with no load, and the maximum electromotive force is 1.3 V. Wikipedia gives a safe operating range of −20 to 45 °C. Self-discharge is about 10% per month at 20 °C and up to 20% per month at higher temperatures; Battery University adds that NiCd loses 10% in the first 24 hours after charge.

NiCd is the chemistry most associated with memory effect: cells repeatedly recharged after only partial discharge gradually lose usable capacity. Energizer reports a voltage depression of about 150 mV in such cells. Battery University recommends periodic full discharges and notes that affected cells can be rejuvenated.

## Uses

Battery University lists two-way radios, emergency medical equipment, professional video cameras and power tools as long-standing uses, and notes that the airline industry still uses the system. Vented NiCd batteries serve aviation, rail, telecom backup and engine starting, with lives of up to 20 years or more and operation from −40 to 70 °C. Consumer cells were made in sizes from AAA to D and as 9 V equivalents.

## History

Waldemar Jungner of Sweden built the first NiCd battery in 1899. Production in the United States began in 1946, and in 1947 a method of absorbing the gases generated during charge led to the modern sealed cell. As of 2000, about 1.5 billion NiCd batteries were produced each year, and until the mid-1990s they held most of the market for rechargeable batteries in home electronics. EU Directive 2006/66/EC limits portable batteries to 0.002% cadmium by weight; the exemption for cordless power tools ended on December 31, 2016.

## Status

Legacy. Battery University describes NiCd as limited to specialty applications because of environmental regulation. IEC uses the letter K for nickel-cadmium (IEC 61951-1).
strengths: Rugged and forgiving if abused (Battery University)
Can be ultra-fast charged with little stress (Battery University)
limitations: Cadmium is toxic and restricted in the EU
Memory effect; needs periodic full discharge
High self-discharge, about 10% per month at 20 °C
Lower specific energy than NiMH and lithium-ion
safety: Cadmium is a toxic metal and cannot be disposed of in landfills
Vented cells release oxygen and hydrogen when overcharged or discharged rapidly
